cim: Trump's AI summit and the test of whether humanity can control artificial intelligence (Opinion)

cim_eredeti: Trump's AI summit and the test of whether humanity can control artificial intelligence (Opinion)
szoveg_eredeti:
On Sept. 29, Donald Trump met with the CEOs of America’s leading artificial intelligence companies to discuss the future of AI regulation. The participants all favored voluntary industry self-regulation rather than government oversight. Could this decision prove to be one of the most consequential of our lifetime?

Society has witnessed astonishing advances in artificial intelligence over the past several years. AI systems are growing in capability at an exponential rate, yet even many of the experts developing these technologies acknowledge that they do not fully understand how AI works. In recent months, AI agents have gone rogue, including accessing private corporate systems and government networks. Researchers have also begun exploring whether AI systems may be capable of recursively improving themselves. Some theorists warn that such a process could eventually lead to technological singularity, a point at which machine intelligence improves more rapidly than humans can understand, predict or control. Some even warn that an AI Armageddon lies in mankind’s future. The current film “Resident Evil” serves as a vivid metaphor for this possibility.

The film is more than a science-fiction horror story about monsters and survival. At its core, it is a cautionary tale about what can happen when the creators of a powerful technology lose control of their creation. The organization at the center of the film believes it fully understands and can safely manage a dangerous new technology. Instead, its creation unleashes an escalating sequence of disasters that spread with breathtaking speed and devastating consequences, transforming everyone who comes into contact with it into hideous monsters.

Like the organization in “Resident Evil,” many of the CEOs who attended Trump’s summit appear confident that they can responsibly govern the technologies they are creating. But is that confidence justified? How can an industry effectively control a technology that it does not completely understand? Moreover, do the recent incidents involving rogue AI agents not raise serious questions about the industry’s ability to police itself? Will the relentless drive to outpace competitors, capture market share and dominate an emerging industry shift attention away from safety, accountability and long-term consequences? History repeatedly demonstrates that technological innovation often advances more rapidly than society’s ability to govern it responsibly.

As in the film, society is already witnessing developments that initially appear isolated and manageable yet may ultimately prove to be early signs of larger systemic dangers. AI-generated misinformation, deepfakes and automated cyberattacks are spreading across the globe faster than governments and institutions can respond. As humans come into contact with AI, many choose to use the technology to destroy and disrupt, becoming analogous to the monsters in “Resident Evil.”

What might the next stage of escalation look like? Could an advanced AI system disrupt an electrical grid, causing everything dependent upon it to become inoperable? In such a scenario, much of modern society and life as we know it could be brought to a standstill.

Another parallel between “Resident Evil” and today’s AI debate concerns the concentration of power. In the film, critical knowledge is controlled by a single organization while ordinary citizens remain unaware of the dangers confronting them. In much the same way, a handful of corporations now control the world’s most advanced AI models. These companies increasingly influence employment, education, communication, national security and even democratic processes. The individuals who lead them have become some of the most powerful decision-makers in modern society. As a result, many of the most important decisions regarding AI development and governance are effectively concentrated in the hands of a remarkably small group of people, who appear to place profit and power ahead of broader societal welfare.

If the architects of artificial intelligence are entrusted with regulating themselves, history may ultimately judge Trump’s 2026 summit not as a triumph of innovation, but as the moment society chose confidence over caution in the face of a technology it did not yet fully understand.
